title: Do You Need Finance or Consulting to Get an MBA?
summary: An early-format episode with roses-and-thorns, a forced ranking of Zoom-call archetypes, and a mailbag question from a 21-year-old about which career paths lead to a top MBA. The sisters reframe the question around what admissions offices are optimizing for, explain why consulting, finance and big tech are the main feeder industries, and offer advice for non-traditional applicants; they end by disagreeing on whether to follow your passion or pragmatically mold your career toward business school.

ideas.idea: To understand which industries feed into top MBAs, flip the question and ask what an admissions director is optimizing for: business schools are institutions that need successful, donating alumni.
ideas.detail: Schools want alumni who become heads of state or make enough money to give back, so they look to industries that train people to think strategically and lead. Admissions is portfolio construction: enough conventional 'sure bets' (e.g. finance) plus some potential outlier successes in each class.

ideas.idea: The three main feeder industries into business school today are management consulting (MBB), finance (especially investment banking and private equity) and big tech.
ideas.detail: Within finance the hosts list banking, PE, VC, hedge funds, long-only, fixed income, endowments and less commonly corporate finance; big tech means the FAANG companies plus Microsoft, which has taken off since Azure and Satya Nadella. Tech is treated separately from startups.

ideas.idea: Consultants are prized by business schools because they have seen a breadth of industries and are trained to structure and enumerate their thinking into digestible recommendations.
ideas.detail: The running joke in Jean's HBS class was consultants starting every answer with 'when I was at McKinsey' and 'there are three things.' In their first two years consultants rotate across oil, healthcare and tech projects and learn to pull strategic themes across them.

ideas.idea: If you are graduating and don't know what you want to do, consulting is one of the top options to pursue because of the industry exposure it gives.
ideas.detail: Cherie recommends it for new grads and undergrads considering internships precisely because it lets you learn many industries and ways of building strategy before committing.

ideas.idea: Finance signals to admissions that you are smart (quantitative skills) and that you have survived a high-pressure environment with an expectation of excellence.
ideas.detail: Jean recalls that in finance everyone believed every deliverable was the end of the world even though half the deadlines were self-imposed; the quantitative bar is an indicator of academic prowess rather than a predictor of success.

ideas.idea: Employers and schools hire from consulting and finance as shorthand for rigorous training: the person has been vetted multiple times and will present and behave professionally even in unrelated roles.
ideas.detail: Because getting an offer at McKinsey, Bain or Goldman is so competitive, the name serves as a proxy that the candidate has gone through 'boot camp' and their work will meet a high bar.

ideas.idea: Your first five years out of school shape your professional habits permanently; as a hiring manager you can see someone's career upbringing in their work product.
ideas.detail: Ex-consultants are consummately professional while startup-raised people are scrappy and fast but hand in memos with typos. Jean says she could never submit work with typos after years of 100-hour weeks being her North Star of quality, though whether typos matter depends on company culture.

ideas.idea: Tech became a major MBA feeder in the last 10-15 years because schools saw outsized startup outcomes and wanted to recruit the next Mark Pincus.
ideas.detail: Pincus, founder and CEO of Zynga (Farmville), went to HBS, which is where Jean worked before business school. Both HBS and GSB have expanded their startup curricula, drawing big-tech employees who want a traditional business foundation and exposure to startups.

ideas.idea: Non-traditional applicants (energy, healthcare, CPG, military, teachers) should still apply but must craft a narrative showing strategic thinking, team leadership and the impact they want to create.
ideas.detail: CPG is only about 5% of the class at Stanford GSB. Be very specific about why you need business school for your goals and why each particular school, e.g. Stanford's entrepreneurship program and cross-registration at the d.school, so admissions doesn't have to extrapolate what they get out of admitting you.

ideas.idea: If your industry lacks MBA role models, find alumni who made the leap and talk to them, because your seniors may not even know how to write a compelling business school recommendation.
ideas.detail: At LinkedIn many of Jean's directors and VPs had MBAs, so she could see the path; friends in traditional engineering who followed their passion were not set up for top programs partly because of the recommendation X-factor.

ideas.idea: Careers are long and business school is only one chapter, so follow your passion and treat an MBA as a bonus rather than sacrificing five unhappy years to get in.
ideas.detail: Cherie, the self-described romantic, argues that finding an industry you are excited to wake up for is the successful start, and if it happens to be consulting, finance or tech, all the better.

ideas.idea: If getting into a top business school is genuinely your goal, it is legitimate to mold your career toward the feeder industries because that is simply where the odds are best.
ideas.detail: Jean, the pragmatist, notes that schools rely on the vetting shorthand of those industries and that outsiders face structural disadvantages, so the truth is you are in a better position in one of the big three.

ideas.idea: Infrastructure and behind-the-scenes work is thankless because it is only noticed when something breaks, so its success criteria are effectively reversed.
ideas.detail: Cherie draws the analogy from doing all the podcast's tech setup to infra and security teams and backend PMs in tech who get all the blame when something goes wrong and no credit when it runs smoothly.

ideas.idea: In large meetings where you are not a key player, multitasking is fine and back-channeling is actually part of doing the meeting well, but never go camera-off and away from keyboard without notice when you may be called on.
ideas.detail: From the forced ranking of Zoom archetypes: roughly 90% of people multitask in 30-plus-person meetings; if you are in an important meeting you should be back-channeling; leaving without warning when the meeting leader needs you ranks as the worst offense.

ideas.idea: Sleep is foundational to health, aging and memory, and a night-owl schedule inherited from early finance and tech jobs is hard to unwind.
ideas.detail: Jean's natural sleep window is 1:30am to 9:30am, a habit from working 10am to midnight at her first jobs; she uses magnesium glycinate, no caffeine after 2pm and melatonin as a last resort. Cherie, citing Andrew Huberman, says put the phone away in bed.
